rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Projectile motion is the superposition of constant horizontal velocity and vertical free fall, giving a parabolic path. The three headline results — $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$, $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — all follow from the component equations, with maximum range at 45° and equal ranges at complementary angles.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Components: $v_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant); $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$
Time of flight: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$
Maximum height: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Independence of Components:** Horizontal motion (constant $v_x = u\cos heta$) and vertical motion (free fall $v_y = u\sin heta - gt$) are completely independent. They share only the time variable $t$. This is the foundational principle — no horizontal force means $v_x$ is constant.  ·  **Trajectory is a Parabola:** Eliminating $t$ gives $y = x an heta - rac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2 heta}$, a downward-opening parabola. This assumes no air resistance, constant $g$, and flat ground. With drag, the trajectory is not a parabola and range decreases.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: In horizontal-launch problems, get the time from the VERTICAL fall first, then multiply by $v_x$.  ·  Note 2: Memorise $\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$ and $\sin 2\theta$ values for 30°/45°/60° — NEB numericals use them constantly.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1 (horizontal launch): a stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m tower: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 20/10} = 2$ s; lands 30 m out — vertical fall sets the TIME, horizontal speed sets the DISTANCE.  ·  Example 2 (full trajectory): $u = 25$ m/s at $\theta = 37°$ ($\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$): $T = 3$ s, $H = 11.25$ m, $R = 60$ m — the classic 3-4-5 projectile.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'A projectile's horizontal velocity decreases during flight.' ✅ $v_x = u\cos\theta$ is CONSTANT (no horizontal force in the ideal model); only $v_y$ changes.  ·  ❌ 'At the top of the trajectory the velocity is zero.' ✅ Only $v_y = 0$; the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ persists — speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$, the MINIMUM of the flight.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Derive $T$, $H$, $R$ from components in writing, then specialise to $\theta = 45°$.  ·  Task 2: Solve ten numericals: horizontal launches, angled launches, and velocity-at-time/height cases.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — for 30° and 60°, $\sin 2\theta = \sin 60° = 0.866$; write the common range instantly.  ·  Trick 2: At 45°, $R = 4H$ — if a question gives one, the other is a division away.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Show that the path of a projectile is a parabola by eliminating $t$ from the equations of motion.  ·  Q2. Derive $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ and hence prove that the range is maximum for $\theta = 45°$.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: Derivations of $T$, $H$ and $R$ from components are standard 4-mark questions — write the two component tables first.  ·  Exam Tip 2: Draw the trajectory with $v_x$ arrows equal everywhere and $v_y$ arrows shrinking/rising — examiners look for the independence idea.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Independence of horizontal (uniform) and vertical (accelerated) motions.  ·  Concept 2: Component kinematics — $v_x$ constant, $v_y$ with $-gt$; time is the shared variable.  ·  Concept 3: Standard results: $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$, $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$.  ·  Concept 4: Symmetry — equal speeds at equal heights; landing mirrors launching.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent; they share only TIME.  ·  $v_x$ is constant; $v_y$ changes by $g$ every second; the path is a parabola.  ·  At the top: $v_y = 0$, speed $= u\cos\theta$ (minimum), $a = g$ downward.  ·  Landing speed equals launch speed; landing angle equals −launch angle (symmetry).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Galileo's *Dialogues* (1638) first showed projectile motion is a parabola by superposing uniform horizontal motion with vertical fall — the first known composition of motions.  ·  Artillery fire above ~30 km (Paris Gun, WWI) deviates from the parabola: thin air changes drag and $g$'s direction varies — ideal parabolic flight is a near-Earth, no-air model.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Show that two angles of projection differing by 90° give the same horizontal range.  ·  Q4. A projectile is fired at 50 m/s at 60°. Find (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height, (c) velocity after 2 s.  ·  Q5. Show that the relation between range and maximum height is $R = 4H\cot\theta$, and verify it for $\theta = 45°$ where $R = 4H$.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: For 'velocity at height h' questions use $v_y^2 = (u\sin\theta)^2 - 2gh$ — avoids solving a quadratic in $t$.  ·  Exam Tip 4: State the no-air-resistance assumption; if a question mentions drag, the parabola model no longer applies.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3 (velocity at top): speed at the top $= u\cos\theta = 20$ m/s for the previous shot — the projectile is never at rest.  ·  Example 4 (45° range): maximum range with $u = 30$ m/s is $R_{max} = u^2/g = 90$ m at 45°, with $H = R/4 = 22.5$ m — note $R_{max} = 4H$.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The horizontal component of a projectile's velocity during ideal flight is: → B  ·  Maximum range for a given launch speed occurs at: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version builds projectile motion from the independence of the two components and derives all standard results step by step — the derivation chain NEB expects.  ·  **The governing idea:** horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT. Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity stays constant ($v_x = u\cos\theta$) while the vertical motion is free fall with initial speed $u\sin\theta$. The path is the combination — a parabola.  ·  **Component equations (up positive, launch at angle $\theta$ with speed $u$):** horizontal: $x = (u\cos\theta)t$, $v_x = u\cos\theta$; vertical: $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Trajectory parabola and the $R$–$H$ relation $R = 4H\cot\theta$.  ·  Range: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$; $R_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ at $\theta = 45°$  ·  Trajectory: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ (parabola); $R = 4H\cot\theta$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Symmetry and Range Maxima:** Time of flight $T = rac{2u\sin heta}{g}$, max height $H = rac{u^2\sin^2 heta}{2g}$, range $R = rac{u^2\sin 2 heta}{g}$. Maximum range at $ heta = 45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($ heta$ and $90^\circ- heta$) give identical ranges because $\sin 2 heta = \sin(180^\circ-2 heta)$.…  ·  $R$ is maximum at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges but different heights.  ·  $R \propto u^2$ and $H \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed quadruples both.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'The path is part of a circle / straight line decaying.' ✅ The trajectory is a PARABOLA — the graph of $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$.  ·  ❌ Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin 2\theta$ in the range. ✅ $R = u^2\sin 2\theta/g$; and $\sin 2\theta$ is maximal at $\theta = 45°$, not $90°$.  ·  ❌ 'Complementary angles give different ranges.' ✅ $\sin 2(90°-\theta) = \sin(180°-2\theta) = \sin 2\theta$ — $30°$ and $60°$ land at the SAME spot (the 60° shot flies higher).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Doubling $u$ doubles the range. ✅ $R \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed QUADRUPLES range (and quadruples max height too).  ·  Example 5 (bomb release): a plane at 500 m flying level at 100 m/s releases a bomb — it lands after $t = 10$ s, $500$ m ahead of the release point (it keeps the plane's horizontal velocity).  ·  Note 3: 'Same range' pairs: compare heights as $\sin^2\theta : \sin^2(90°-\theta)$ — the steeper shot rises 3× higher for the 30°/60° pair.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 4: State the assumptions (no air resistance, constant $g$, flat ground) in theory answers — they define the model.  ·  Note 1: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal: $v = u\cos\theta$ — not zero.  ·  Note 2: Landing speed equals launch speed and the landing angle mirrors the launch angle (energy/symmetry).
